stem: A 64-year-old woman has had headaches for 25 years and takes several tablets of one of her medications every day. She now has flank pain and passes blood in her urine. Blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg, creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. CT shows small kidneys with sloughed tissue in the renal pelvis. She also takes digoxin, nifedipine, propranolol and warfarin.
oneliner: 64F + 25 y headaches + several tablets of one drug daily + hematuria, flank pain + Cr 2.4 + sterile pyuria + small kidneys with sloughed papillae + also digoxin, nifedipine, propranolol, warfarin → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused her kidney disease?

whyNot.A: **Cardiac glycoside**: toxicity gives arrhythmias and visual changes, not papillary necrosis
whyNot.B: **Dihydropyridine**: causes edema and flushing, not kidney damage
whyNot.C: **Beta-blocker**: bradycardia and bronchospasm, not kidney damage
whyNot.D: **Anticoagulant**: bleeding is the danger; does not cause papillary necrosis

why: **Years of high daily analgesic use + sterile pyuria + small kidneys + sloughed papillae** = analgesic nephropathy with papillary necrosis, caused by chronic **aspirin / NSAID** use.

drug.name: Aspirin (NSAIDs)
drug.how: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2, lowering prostaglandins and thromboxane
drug.use: Analgesia, antipyresis, antiplatelet therapy, Kawasaki disease
drug.watch: Gastric ulcers, tinnitus, analgesic nephropathy and papillary necrosis, Reye syndrome in children, respiratory alkalosis then anion gap acidosis in overdose

stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction takes lisinopril and furosemide. His cardiologist adds spironolactone. Two weeks later he feels weak, and his creatinine has crept up. The ECG shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves.
oneliner: 68M + HFrEF on lisinopril, furosemide + spironolactone added 2 wk ago + weakness, creatinine up + peaked T waves → which electrolyte problem?
ask: Which of the following electrolyte disturbances most likely developed?

whyNot.A: Aldosterone blockade **retains** potassium; low K+ would flatten T waves and add U waves
whyNot.C: Low sodium does not **peak the T waves**; that ECG change points to potassium
whyNot.D: Aldosterone blockade gives a **mild acidosis** (less H+ secretion), the opposite of alkalosis
whyNot.E: Not linked to these drugs, and it would **shorten the QT**, not peak the T waves

why: **Peaked T waves** with weakness point to high potassium. **Spironolactone blocks aldosterone** in the collecting duct so K+ is not secreted, and the **ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone** further; falling renal function adds to the load.

drug.name: Spironolactone
drug.how: Blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct, so less Na+ is reabsorbed and less K+ and H+ are secreted
drug.use: HFrEF (mortality benefit), resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, ascites, hirsutism
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia (worse with ACE inhibitor, ARB, CKD), gynecomastia, antiandrogen effects

idea.rule: Anything that lowers aldosterone action or blocks distal K+ secretion can cause hyperkalemia.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with idiopathic intracranial hypertension has taken acetazolamide for 2 years. She now has colicky right flank pain. This is her first stone, and no relative has had stones. Her urine pH is 7.5 on repeated tests, urinalysis shows no bacteria, and serum calcium is normal. Plain x-ray shows a radiopaque stone.
oneliner: 34F + idiopathic intracranial hypertension on acetazolamide 2 y + colicky flank pain + urine pH 7.5 + no bacteria + radiopaque stone → which stone?
ask: Which of the following types of stone is most likely?

whyNot.A: Uric acid precipitates in **acidic** urine, and it is **radiolucent**; her pH is 7.5 and the stone is radiopaque
whyNot.C: Cystine stones come from an **inherited transport defect**; she has a first stone at 34 and **no family history**
whyNot.D: Struvite needs **urease-producing bacteria**; her urine shows **no bacteria**
whyNot.E: Xanthine stones are extremely rare and **radiolucent**; hers is **radiopaque**

why: **Acetazolamide** blocks carbonic anhydrase, so bicarbonate is lost and the **urine becomes alkaline (pH 7.5)**; it also lowers urinary citrate. **Calcium phosphate** precipitates in alkaline urine and appears radiopaque.

drug.name: Acetazolamide
drug.how: Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so bicarbonate is lost in urine; urine turns alkaline and citrate falls
drug.use: Acute mountain sickness prevention, glaucoma, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, metabolic alkalosis
drug.watch: Calcium phosphate stones, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, sulfonamide allergy cross-reactivity

idea.rule: Alkaline urine favors calcium phosphate and struvite stones; acidic urine favors uric acid and cystine stones.
also: Topiramate, a weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, also causes calcium phosphate stones
Proteus infection makes ammonia and alkaline urine, giving struvite stones
Low urinary citrate promotes calcium stones; potassium citrate treats it
Renal tubular acidosis type 1 makes alkaline urine and calcium phosphate stones

stem: A 35-year-old woman with long-standing asthma cannot urinate 2 days after a vaginal delivery. Her bladder is distended and catheterization drains 800 mL. There is no obstruction on examination. Her obstetrician considers starting bethanechol but pauses because of her asthma.
oneliner: 35F + long-standing asthma + 2 days postpartum + cannot void, 800 mL on catheterization + no obstruction + bethanechol considered → which drug action is both reason and caution?
ask: Which of the following drug actions is both the reason to use bethanechol and the reason for caution here?

whyNot.A: This would worsen asthma but **cannot make the atonic bladder contract**
whyNot.B: Bethanechol does not inhibit the enzyme: it is **resistant to cholinesterase**
whyNot.C: Histamine causes **bronchospasm**, but bethanechol does not act on histamine receptors and does not empty the bladder
whyNot.E: Would block transmission rather than **contract the bladder**, and bethanechol is not a nicotinic blocker

why: **Postpartum urinary retention with an atonic bladder and no obstruction** is the setting for bethanechol, a **muscarinic agonist** that contracts the detrusor through **M3 receptors**. The same M3 stimulation **constricts bronchial smooth muscle**, so it is risky in **asthma**.

drug.name: Bethanechol
drug.how: Stimulates M3 receptors, contracting the detrusor; resistant to cholinesterase, with little nicotinic action
drug.use: Postoperative and postpartum urinary retention, neurogenic bladder atony
drug.watch: Bronchoconstriction (avoid in asthma), bradycardia, salivation, sweating, diarrhea; contraindicated with obstruction

idea.rule: A drug's benefit and its harm can come from the same receptor: M3 stimulation contracts the bladder and the bronchi.
also: Methacholine challenge uses muscarinic bronchoconstriction to diagnose asthma
Cholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine also worsen bronchospasm
Bethanechol is also contraindicated with mechanical urinary or bowel obstruction
Bradycardia and increased gastric acid are further muscarinic effects
